newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu, Arafat speak by phone amid tensions.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu, Arafat speak by phone amid tensions.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent envoys to Yasser Arafat and later spoke by phone to the Palestinian president after tensions flared over government benefits for Jewish settlers in the West Bank.
A statement issued by Netanyahu's office after the telephone conversation late on Sunday, stepping around the burning topic of the day, did not mention the word "settlements" once.
"The prime minister said both sides must act against terror and continue to make progress in negotiations for peace," it said.

Netanyahu sent cabinet secretary Danny Naveh and adviser Yitzhak Molcho to meet Arafat in self-ruled Gaza for the highest-level talks between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation in weeks.
Arafat earlier reacted angrily to the Israeli government's decision to grant financial benefits, such as tax breaks, to West Bank settlers.

"Instead of implementing what the (peace) agreements demand, they decide to expand settlements. Netanyahu knows that's a time bomb with many risks," the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth quoted Arafat as saying.

The Palestinian Information Ministry has described the Israeli move as a declaration of war. About 130,000 Jews now live amid two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, areas captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

Netanyahu accused Palestinians of plotting violence even before he reinstated the financial incentives, cancelled by the Labour-led government he defeated in elections last May, for Jews to settle in the West Bank.
"I think (Arafat) has to understand that we'll not sit with folded hands when faced with such threats," Netanyahu told Army Radio.

Israeli-PLO violence last flared seriously in September when Israel's opening of an entrance to a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem led to clashes in which 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
The statement issued by Netanyahu's office focused on "terrorism", four days after Arab militants shot dead a Jewish settler and her 12-year-old son in the West Bank.

It said Naveh and Molcho spoke to Arafat about the need for the Palestinian self-rule Authority to "fight terror and especially the terror of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine," which claimed responsibility for the shooting.

"During the meeting, Arafat telephoned Prime Minister Netanyahu and expressed his sorrow at the murder of the Tzur family from Beit El last week. Arafat said he also demanded the PFLP stop terror," it said.

It also said Netanyahu expressed his condolences to Arafat over the killing by a Jewish farmer in southern Israel of a Palestinian worker from Gaza on Thursday. The Israeli told police he believed the Gazan was a "terrorist".
The Palestinian Authority had no immediate comment on the meeting and telephone call or on the statement's attributing to Arafat the use of the word "terror" to describe the PFLP attack.
Molcho has been a key middleman in low-profile contacts with the PLO on breaking a deadlock in U.S.-mediated talks on a long overdue Israeli troop redeployment in Hebron in the West Bank.

"The prime minister added (in his conversation with Arafat) that he believes it is possible to wind up the Hebron matter soon and then chart out the continuation of the peace process," the statement said.

Netanyahu has accused Arafat of delaying a Hebron agreement in hope of portraying Israel as a reluctant peace partner and bringing world pressure on the Jewish state. Arafat has denied the allegation.
